thesis: This episode argues that Charlie Munger's investment journey into Berkshire Hathaway generated extraordinary returns (1,500x) because he entered a great growing business at a low price, contrasting this with the 'auction-driven' market where valuations like Meta's changed dramatically. It suggests that holding major S&P 500 constituents like Microsoft and Apple for a long time provides an edge, while noting that Munger's specific entry into Belridge Oil was a low-price asset play that Shell later bought at a premium.

claims.claim: The S&P 500 index holds Microsoft for a long time, which is an edge.
claims.quote: The index is too dumb to know that it owns Microsoft. It's too dumb to know that it owns alphabet. And it's too dumb to sell these things. And it keeps these things endlessly forever.

claims.claim: The S&P 500 index holds Alphabet for a long time, which is an edge.
claims.quote: The index is too dumb to know that it owns Microsoft. It's too dumb to know that it owns alphabet. And it's too dumb to sell these things. And it keeps these things endlessly forever.

claims.claim: The S&P 500 index holds Amazon for a long time, which is an edge.
claims.quote: The S&P 500 would hold an Apple or Microsoft or Amazon or Alphabet for 20 years, 30 years. And that type of holding period on these great businesses can be a great edge.

claims.claim: The S&P 500 index holds Apple for a long time, which is an edge.
claims.quote: The S&P 500 would hold an Apple or Microsoft or Amazon or Alphabet for 20 years, 30 years. And that type of holding period on these great businesses can be a great edge.

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway was trading at about $300 a share in 1979.
claims.quote: And at that time in 79, Berkshire Hathaway was trading at about $300 a share or something, which is now approaching a half a million dollars a share.

claims.claim: Meta's valuation changed dramatically in 2022, showing the auction-driven nature of the market.
claims.quote: In 2022, we saw a lot of overshooting, right? A lot of high flyers, a lot of great businesses got really a year ago, for whatever reason, these auction participants gave Facebook slash Meta Labs a certain valuation. And then by the end of the year, they had taken it out back and shot it.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger bought Belridge Oil at a very low price relative to its assets.
claims.quote: And Charlie said that without even doing much of an analysis, you knew there you were buying it for one-fifth or one-tenth or one-tenth or less of what the actual underlying assets were worth.

claims.claim: Shell Oil bought Belridge Oil for 3.5 billion two years after Munger declined to buy it.
claims.quote: And he said that, so two years later, this 100 million market cap company was bought by Shell Oil for 3.5 billion. And it was like 30x or something, $120 million or something.

claims.claim: The $30,000 Charlie Munger invested in Berkshire Hathaway became $1.5 billion today.
claims.quote: So the $30,000 in effect became $1.5 billion, $35,000.

claims.claim: The journey from Berkshire Hathaway was a cross-connect where you take a first company and then you get a 30x, and then you take the second company, and in his case, he got a 1,500X.
claims.quote: So you end up with 45,000 X, some crazy number like that.

claims.claim: The second company Charlie Munger invested in Berkshire Hathaway was a great growing business.
claims.quote: And that was now the second company that he invested in Berkshire Hathaway was a great growing business. And that generated a lot of the returns because of the growth.
